front: Which GYN cancers are driven by HPV, and which is driven by estrogen?
back: HPV: cervical, vaginal, and many vulvar cancers. Estrogen: endometrioid endometrial cancer.
extra: Endometrial cancer is heterogeneous: serous and p53-abnormal tumors are not estrogen-driven. Ovarian cancer is the genetic one (BRCA, Lynch) and is treated mainly with surgery and chemo, not radiation.

front: Besides HPV infection itself, what raises the risk of cervical cancer?
back: Smoking and immunosuppression (which keep HPV from clearing), more HPV exposure, and above all lack of screening
extra: The HPV vaccine prevents new infections but does not clear existing ones, so vaccinated women are still screened. Nearly all cervical cancers start in the transformation zone, where glandular canal cells meet the squamous outer cervix.

front: What single mechanism explains most risk factors for endometrioid endometrial cancer?
back: Unopposed estrogen (estrogen stimulating the lining without progesterone)
extra: Obesity, nulliparity, PCOS, unopposed HRT, and tamoxifen. Serous and p53-abnormal tumors are the exception: not estrogen-driven.

front: What is the classic presentation of endometrial cancer, and why is it usually caught early?
back: Postmenopausal bleeding, which prompts an early workup (transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial biopsy)
extra: An endometrial stripe >4 mm in a postmenopausal woman needs a biopsy.

front: Why is every endometrial cancer tested for mismatch repair (MMR/MSI)?
back: To screen for Lynch syndrome, and because MMR-deficient tumors respond well to immunotherapy
extra: Lynch carries a 30-60% lifetime endometrial cancer risk. A young patient with a family history of colon cancer is the classic case.

front: Why do women who received the HPV vaccine still need cervical cancer screening?
back: The vaccine prevents new infections but does not clear existing ones, and it does not cover every cancer-causing type.
extra: Screening uses cytology and/or HPV testing to find precancer before it becomes cancer.

front: How do serous and p53-abnormal endometrial cancers differ from endometrioid cancer?
back: They are not estrogen-driven, occur in older and often thinner patients, spread early (peritoneum), and carry a poor prognosis even when confined to the uterus.
extra: They often need more aggressive adjuvant therapy (chemotherapy ± RT).

front: Which endometrial molecular group has a very low recurrence risk even when high grade?
back: POLE-mutated tumors
extra: They are candidates for de-escalation of adjuvant therapy. p53-abnormal tumors are the most aggressive.

front: What are the two pathways to vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, and which has the worse prognosis?
back: HPV-associated (younger women, usual-type VIN) and HPV-independent (older women, arising in lichen sclerosus). The HPV-independent, p53-mutated type has the worse prognosis.
extra: Biopsy any persistent vulvar lesion, because many are treated for months as irritation.

front: How does tamoxifen affect endometrial cancer risk, and why?
back: It raises the risk, because tamoxifen acts as an estrogen agonist in the uterus.
extra: Combined oral contraceptives, a progestin IUD, and pregnancy are protective.

front: Why can a cervical cancer that grows sideways cause hydronephrosis?
back: The ureter runs through the parametrium, under the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix, so lateral tumor can squeeze it.
extra: "Water under the bridge." Hydronephrosis from tumor makes it stage IIIB.

front: Which part of the vagina drains to the groin nodes?
back: The lower third (like the vulva)
extra: The upper two-thirds drain to the pelvic nodes like the cervix, so lower-third involvement adds the groins to the field.

front: In what order does cervical cancer spread through the lymph nodes?
back: Pelvic nodes (parametrial, obturator, internal and external iliac) first, then common iliac, then para-aortic
extra: Endometrial cancer follows the same path but can also jump straight to the para-aortics along the ovarian vessels.

front: Where does vulvar cancer spread first, and what does a positive pelvic node mean?
back: To the inguinofemoral (groin) nodes. A pelvic node is distant (stage IVB) for the vulva.
extra: Lateral tumors drain to one groin; midline tumors (clitoris, perineum) drain to both. Two pathways to vulvar cancer: HPV-associated (younger women) and HPV-independent from lichen sclerosus (older, p53-mutated, worse prognosis).

front: What is the most common site of recurrence after hysterectomy for endometrial cancer, and how is it treated preventively?
back: The vaginal cuff; it is the target of adjuvant vaginal brachytherapy.
extra: The cuff is the sewn-closed top of the vagina after hysterectomy.

front: Where does nearly every cervical cancer start, and why are most of them squamous?
back: The transformation zone, where the glandular cells of the canal meet the squamous cells of the outer cervix. HPV damages these squamous cells.
extra: A minority of cervical cancers are adenocarcinomas from the glandular canal.

front: What is the parametrium, and what runs through it?
back: The fatty tissue around the cardinal ligament, between the cervix and the pelvic side wall. It carries the uterine artery, the ureter, and lymphatics.
extra: Cervical cancer grows sideways into the parametria, which is why the rectovaginal exam and MRI focus there.

front: How can an endometrial cancer reach the para-aortic nodes without passing through the pelvic nodes?
back: From the fundus, directly along the ovarian vessels
extra: Endometrial cancer otherwise drains to the pelvic nodes like the cervix.

front: Which normal organ most often limits the cervical brachytherapy dose, and which is easy to forget?
back: The rectum most often limits the dose. The sigmoid is easy to forget because it can loop over the tip of the tandem.
extra: The bladder also receives dose from both EBRT and brachytherapy.

front: Why does a midline vulvar cancer need both groins evaluated?
back: Lymph from midline structures (clitoris, perineal body) drains to both groins.
extra: A lesion 2 cm or more from the midline drains mainly to the same-side groin.

front: Which imaging tests stage cervical cancer locally vs for nodes and distant disease?
back: Pelvic MRI (T2) for local extent; FDG PET/CT for nodes and distant disease
extra: FIGO 2018 lets imaging assign the cervical stage.

front: On cervical MRI, what finding indicates parametrial invasion, and why does it change treatment?
back: A break in the dark (low-signal) cervical stromal ring with tumor extending into the parametrial fat. That is stage IIB, treated with chemoradiation rather than radical hysterectomy.
extra: An intact stromal ring essentially rules out parametrial invasion. Tumor is intermediate gray on T2.

front: In cervical cancer, what PET/CT finding usually extends the radiation field above the pelvis?
back: Para-aortic (or high-risk common iliac) nodal uptake, which leads to an extended field covering the para-aortic chain
extra: PET changes the radiation map: a PET-positive pelvic node gets a boost, and distant disease can change the treatment intent.

front: What does the HR-CTV represent in cervical brachytherapy, and why is it imaged at each insertion?
back: The whole cervix plus any residual tumor at the time of brachytherapy. The tumor shrinks during EBRT, so the target is redrawn on MRI or CT with each applicator placement.
extra: A common goal is HR-CTV D90 of at least 85 Gy EQD2 (EBRT plus brachy combined).

front: What is point A in cervical brachytherapy?
back: The historical prescription point, 2 cm up and 2 cm lateral along the tandem, near where the ureter crosses under the uterine artery
extra: Modern image-guided brachytherapy prescribes to the HR-CTV, but point A is still reported for comparison.

front: On MRI of endometrial cancer, which two findings matter most?
back: Depth of myometrial invasion (less than half vs half or more) and whether the cervical stroma is involved
extra: MRI is the main staging tool for medically inoperable patients who get definitive RT.

front: What does a post-treatment PET a few months after cervical chemoradiation tell you?
back: Whether the response is complete, which is a strong sign of a good outcome
extra: Persistent uptake raises concern for residual disease.

front: Why is IMRT standard for pelvic GYN radiation?
back: It lowers dose to the bowel and bone marrow compared with 3D treatment.
extra: RTOG 1203 (TIME-C) showed less GI and urinary toxicity with IMRT after hysterectomy.

front: Before applying a site's FIGO system, what do you determine for any GYN cancer?
back: The organ, then the local extent, nodal disease, and distant disease
extra: FIGO stages loosely move outward (organ, adjacent structure, side wall or nodes, mucosa or distant), but each site defines them differently, so always apply the site's own system.

front: In any GYN cancer, what does a positive regional lymph node do to the stage?
back: It makes it at least stage III, no matter how small the primary is.
extra: Example: a 3.8 cm cervical tumor with a positive pelvic node is IIIC1, not IB2.

front: Which GYN cancers are staged clinically and which surgically, and why?
back: Cervix and vagina are staged clinically (exam + imaging), because many patients go straight to chemoradiation. Endometrium and vulva are staged surgically, because the defining facts come from the specimen.
extra: For cervix, pathology supersedes imaging and exam when available (FIGO 2018).

front: What size cutoffs divide cervical cancer stage IB1, IB2, and IB3?
back: IB1 ≤2 cm, IB2 >2-4 cm, IB3 >4 cm
extra: These matter because IB3 (and higher) gets chemoradiation rather than surgery.

front: In cervical cancer, what stage is parametrial invasion, and what pushes it to IIIB?
back: Parametrial invasion = IIB. Extension to the pelvic side wall or hydronephrosis = IIIB.
extra: Upper two-thirds of the vagina = IIA; lower third = IIIA.

front: In cervical cancer, what is the difference between IIIC1 and IIIC2?
back: IIIC1 = pelvic nodes; IIIC2 = para-aortic nodes
extra: Suffix r = found on imaging; p = proven on pathology.

front: Does bullous edema of the bladder make a GYN cancer stage IVA?
back: No. Stage IVA requires biopsy-proven bladder or rectal mucosal invasion.

front: On the anatomic (FIGO 2009) backbone, what separates endometrial stage IA, IB, and II?
back: IA <50% myometrial invasion; IB ≥50%; II = cervical stroma involved
extra: Tumor in the cervical glands alone does not make it stage II. FIGO 2023 builds on these stages by adding histology, LVSI, and molecular group in selected stages.

front: Why does endometrial cancer molecular class matter for adjuvant therapy?
back: It modifies the recurrence risk: POLE-mutated tumors are candidates for de-escalation, and p53-abnormal tumors for escalation.
extra: The other two groups are MMR-deficient (Lynch screening, immunotherapy-responsive) and no specific profile. FIGO 2023 downstages POLE-mutated and upstages p53-abnormal early tumors.

front: What depth cutoffs divide cervical cancer stage IA1 and IA2?
back: IA1 = invasion under 3 mm. IA2 = 3 to under 5 mm. Deeper than 5 mm (or visible) is IB.
extra: IA1 without LVSI needs only a cone or simple hysterectomy.

front: In cervical cancer, what stage is involvement of the lower third of the vagina?
back: IIIA
extra: Upper two-thirds of the vagina without parametria is IIA. Lower-third involvement also adds the groin nodes to the field.

front: Does involvement of the endometrial glands of the cervix make an endometrial cancer stage II?
back: No. Stage II requires invasion of the cervical stroma.
extra: Deep myometrial invasion (≥50%) without stromal involvement is IB.

front: How does FIGO 2023 let molecular class change an early endometrial cancer's stage?
back: For stage I-II only: POLE-mutated tumors are downstaged (IAmPOLEmut), and p53-abnormal tumors with myometrial invasion are upstaged (IICmp53abn).
extra: Stage III-IV are not reclassified by molecular class.

front: What two numbers define stage IA vulvar cancer, and why does that stage matter?
back: 2 cm or smaller and 1 mm or less of invasion. Groin evaluation can be skipped because the nodal risk is under 1%.
extra: Biopsy with a punch or wedge (not excision) so the depth can be measured on intact tissue.

front: How does node size change the stage of vulvar cancer?
back: Nodes 5 mm or smaller = IIIA. Larger than 5 mm = IIIB. Extracapsular spread = IIIC. Fixed or ulcerated nodes = IVA.
extra: Node status is the single most important determinant of vulvar cancer survival.

front: Before staging a tumor as a vaginal cancer, what must you rule out?
back: That it is actually a cervical or vulvar cancer, or a metastasis
extra: By FIGO definition, a tumor touching the cervix is cervical and one touching the vulva is vulvar. Most lesions in the vagina are secondary.

front: What principle guides the choice between surgery and definitive chemoradiation for cervical cancer?
back: Choose the definitive local treatment that avoids unnecessary multimodality toxicity; add adjuvant RT or chemoRT after surgery only when the pathology warrants it.
extra: Small confined tumors: surgery or definitive RT. Locally advanced or known node-positive disease: definitive chemoradiation plus brachytherapy.

front: What is the standard treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer (IB3-IVA)?
back: Pelvic EBRT with concurrent weekly cisplatin, followed by brachytherapy
extra: Pelvic EBRT is typically about 45 Gy in 25 fractions. The 1999 cisplatin trials showed chemoradiation beats RT alone for survival. No routine hysterectomy afterward.

front: Why cannot brachytherapy be replaced by IMRT or SBRT in cervical cancer?
back: Brachytherapy is what delivers the curative dose to the cervix while sparing the bladder and rectum; leaving it out lowers cure rates.
extra: Bulky or parametrial residual tumor gets interstitial needles added. Brachy is planned on MRI (or CT) with the applicator in place; the common goal is HR-CTV D90 ≥85 Gy EQD2 (EBRT + brachy), with bladder, rectum, and sigmoid D2cc limits (EMBRACE).

front: Within what time should cervical chemoradiation plus brachytherapy be completed, and why?
back: Promptly, in about 8 weeks, because prolonged overall treatment time lowers local control
extra: Treatment breaks let the tumor repopulate.

front: What are the curative options for early cervical cancer (e.g., IB1-IB2), and how should surgery be done?
back: Radical hysterectomy with node evaluation, done open, or definitive radiation (EBRT + brachy), with similar survival
extra: LACC: minimally invasive radical hysterectomy had worse survival. SHAPE: simple hysterectomy is enough for low-risk tumors.

front: After radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer, which kinds of features make up the Sedlis criteria, and what do they trigger?
back: Combinations of LVSI, depth of stromal invasion, and tumor size (intermediate risk). They trigger adjuvant pelvic RT.
extra: GOG 92: pelvic RT cut recurrence roughly in half. The exact combinations are in the reading's checker.

front: What are the Peters criteria after radical hysterectomy, and what do they trigger?
back: Positive nodes, positive margins, or parametrial invasion. They trigger adjuvant chemoradiation.
extra: GOG 109: adding chemo to pelvic RT improved overall survival.

front: After hysterectomy for endometrial cancer, how does adjuvant treatment scale with recurrence risk?
back: Low: observation. Intermediate (mostly vaginal cuff risk): vaginal brachytherapy. Higher pelvic risk: pelvic EBRT. High-risk biology or stage III or higher: systemic therapy ± RT.
extra: Risk rises with deep invasion, high grade, substantial LVSI, cervical stromal invasion, and older age. Molecular group adjusts it: POLE-mutated tumors can often be observed; p53-abnormal tumors are escalated.

front: What did PORTEC-2 show?
back: For high-intermediate risk endometrial cancer, vaginal brachytherapy controlled the vagina as well as pelvic EBRT, with far less GI toxicity.
extra: PORTEC-1 / GOG 99: pelvic RT cut recurrence (mostly vaginal) without improving survival.

front: What is the adjuvant approach for stage III (node-positive) endometrial cancer?
back: Chemotherapy-led: carboplatin/paclitaxel ± pelvic (± para-aortic) EBRT ± vaginal brachy
extra: PORTEC-3: chemoRT beat RT alone, mainly stage III and serous. Immunotherapy helps advanced disease, especially MMR-deficient.

front: Which vulvar cancers can skip groin node evaluation?
back: Stage IA only (≤2 cm and ≤1 mm invasion), because the nodal risk is under 1%
extra: Everyone else gets groin evaluation, with sentinel node biopsy for unifocal tumors <4 cm and clinically negative groins (GROINSS-V).

front: After vulvar cancer surgery, what findings call for adjuvant groin and pelvic radiation?
back: Two or more positive nodes, extracapsular extension, or a sentinel node metastasis >2 mm
extra: GOG 37: groin/pelvic RT beat pelvic node dissection for survival. Weekly cisplatin is often added.

front: When is vulvar cancer treated with definitive chemoradiation instead of surgery?
back: When surgery would require exenteration or destroy the urethra, anus, or clitoris
extra: GOG 205: chemoRT with weekly cisplatin gave a high complete response rate. Residual disease is biopsied and resected if feasible.

front: How is a superficial stage I vaginal cancer treated?
back: Brachytherapy alone (vaginal cylinder)
extra: Thicker or more advanced tumors borrow from cervix: EBRT ± cisplatin plus a brachy boost, adding the groins for lower-third tumors. Before staging, confirm a true vaginal primary: a tumor touching the cervix is staged as cervical, one touching the vulva as vulvar, and many vaginal lesions are metastases or recurrences.

front: What kind of radiation is used for heavy vaginal bleeding from an incurable cervical cancer?
back: A short palliative course (e.g., 8 Gy × 1-3, 20 Gy in 5, or a twice-daily "quad shot")
extra: Choose by prognosis and goals.

front: What are the common acute side effects of pelvic chemoradiation for GYN cancers?
back: Diarrhea, cystitis, fatigue, and low blood counts (from cisplatin plus marrow dose)
extra: IMRT lowers GI, urinary, and marrow toxicity compared with 3D (TIME-C). Vulvar and groin fields add a skin reaction.

front: What late vaginal side effect follows GYN radiation, and how is it prevented?
back: Vaginal stenosis (narrowing and dryness), prevented with regular dilator use
extra: Other late effects: ovarian failure (consider ovarian transposition in young patients), bowel/bladder injury, fistula, insufficiency fractures, lymphedema.

front: What did the LACC trial show about radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer?
back: Minimally invasive (laparoscopic or robotic) surgery gave worse disease-free and overall survival than open surgery.
extra: This is why radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer is done open.

front: Which trials made concurrent cisplatin standard with radiation for locally advanced cervical cancer?
back: The 1999 cisplatin trials (GOG 85, 120, 123, RTOG 9001, SWOG 8797), which showed a substantially lower risk of death
extra: The usual regimen is weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m² during pelvic EBRT.

front: What did GOG 92 and GOG 109 show after radical hysterectomy?
back: GOG 92: pelvic RT for intermediate-risk (Sedlis) features cut recurrence roughly in half. GOG 109: adding chemo to pelvic RT for high-risk (Peters) features improved overall survival.
extra: The two trials define the Sedlis and Peters pathways.

front: What happens if positive nodes are found during a planned radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer?
back: The hysterectomy is often abandoned in favor of definitive chemoradiation, rather than finishing a morbid operation that will need chemoRT anyway.
extra: Triple therapy (radical surgery plus chemoRT) adds toxicity without better cure.

front: What did KEYNOTE-A18 add for high-risk locally advanced cervical cancer?
back: Pembrolizumab during and after chemoradiation improved progression-free and overall survival.
extra: INTERLACE showed a short course of induction carboplatin and paclitaxel before chemoRT also improved survival.

front: What did PORTEC-3 and GOG 258 show for high-risk endometrial cancer?
back: PORTEC-3: chemoRT beat RT alone, mostly in stage III and serous or p53-abnormal tumors. GOG 258: adding RT to chemo lowered vaginal and pelvic recurrences.
extra: High-risk endometrial cancer is treated with combined modality therapy.

front: How is a medically inoperable endometrial cancer treated?
back: Definitive brachytherapy ± EBRT, with MRI to define the extent
extra: Hormonal therapy is an option for selected patients.

front: What did GOG 37 show for node-positive vulvar cancer?
back: Groin and pelvic radiation beat pelvic node dissection.
extra: GOG 205 later showed definitive chemoRT with weekly cisplatin gave high complete response rates in locally advanced disease.

front: How can a central pelvic recurrence of cervical cancer after prior radiation be treated for cure?
back: Pelvic exenteration in selected patients
extra: A pelvic recurrence after surgery alone is treated with chemoradiation ± brachytherapy.

front: What option protects ovarian function in a young woman having surgery who will then need pelvic radiation?
back: Ovarian transposition: moving the ovaries out of the radiation field
extra: Pelvic radiation otherwise causes ovarian failure and premature menopause.
